title: Predicting car prices with Large Tabular Models
summary: A large tabular model priced 1,500 used cars, taken from 14,463 listings from Belgian car dealers, with the lowest mean error of our test: 5.08%. A…
body_markdown:
**Research note**


**5.08%** mean error, lowest of 3 kinds of model


**1,500** test cars


**83 times** cheaper per answer: a fine-tuned small model level with Fable 5.2 at its full price, $41.26 to train, repaid beyond 2,198 answers


November 2026


Picture a table. Each row is one car: brand, model, year, mileage, fuel, power. One more column holds the price the car was listed at. Now take a car the table has never seen and ask a model to fill in that last cell. The same shape fits a claim cost, a flat rent or a customer's yearly spend.


A large tabular model is built for this job. It is pre-trained on many tables, so it reads yours as context and answers with no training of its own. We asked one to price 1,500 used cars, taken from 14,463 listings from Belgian car dealers, snapshot of 16 Nov 2026. We kept the 1,500 cars out of everything we gave any model: the training rows, the examples in the question and the context.


The large tabular model was TabPFN 3.5 Thinking from Prior Labs. Its price was off by 5.08% on average, the lowest mean error of the test. We compared it with two other kinds of model on the same cars: a general model, Fable 5.2 from Anthropic, and a small language model, Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab, fine-tuned on the Tinker service. Without examples the general model was off by 10.09%.


The comparison holds a second result. Given 30 similar cars in each question, Fable 5.2 scored 6.03% and the fine-tuned small model 6.26%, and the test cannot tell those two apart. At Fable's full price the small model costs about 83 times less per answer. It took $41.26 to train and is cheaper in total beyond 2,198 answers. This note shows how we ran the test, what each kind costs and where each goes wrong. It ends with two apps you can try and five moves for Monday.


**The result in one film.** It starts on the answers of three models on the 1,500 test cars, first by brand, then sorted, then as one chart through the five settings: 10.09%, 6.03%, 7.12%, 6.26% and 5.08% mean error. The second half prices one car at 21,666 EUR, with its range, then changes the car. The priced car then turns back into the first picture, and the film loops. The short version


- **A large tabular model priced the cars with the lowest error.** TabPFN 3.5 Thinking had a mean error of 5.08% on 1,500 test cars. 83.9% of its prices landed within 10% of the asking price.
- **A fine-tuned small model is level with Fable 5.2 and about 83 times cheaper per answer.** With 30 similar cars in each question, Inkling 2 Mini scored 6.26% against 6.03% for Fable 5.2, a gap of 0.23 points that the test cannot separate. It costs $0.000228 per answer against $0.019 at Fable's full price, after $41.26 of training, and it is cheaper in total beyond 2,198 answers.
- **A general model needs examples.** Fable 5.2 alone was off by 10.09%. With 30 similar cars in each question it fell to 6.03%, with no training.
- **A bigger model and longer training did not help.** Inkling 2 Small scored 7.15% against 7.12%. Eight passes scored 7.40%. Neither gap is separated from zero.
- **A floor exists.** Cars identical on every input differ in asking price by 1.0% to 2.4%, so an error under 1% is out of reach.
- **Our answer:** start with a tabular model for any prediction from a table. Keep a general model with 30 similar examples as the second option. Fine-tune only when the number of questions repays the training.


## 1


Why this matters


Many business questions have the shape of our car question. You hold a table of past cases with their outcomes. A new case arrives with its outcome missing. You need a number you can act on.


- **The choice sets the bill.** A general model charges for each question. A fine-tuned model charges once to train and little for each question. A tabular model needs no training and can run on your own machine.
- **The choice sets the miss.** In our test the best setting was off by 5.08% and the weakest of five by 10.09%.


We wanted one table, one set of cars and one yardstick for all three kinds.


**So what?** Pick the kind of model by testing it on your own table, with the same cases for every candidate. This note shows how we did it on one table, and what came out.


## 2


The words, explained once


This section assumes you have never trained a model. If you have, skip tosection 3 .


### The car side


- **Asking price.** The price on the listing. It is what the seller wants, which can differ from the price paid.
- **Training cars.** The 11,963 listings a model learns from.
- **Validation cars.** 1,000 listings used to choose between versions of one model.
- **Test cars.** 1,500 listings we kept out of everything we gave the models. Every score here comes from them.


### The error side


- **Mean error.** For each test car, the gap between the model's price and the asking price, as a share of the asking price. The mean error is the average gap. A mean error of 5% means a typical price was 5% too high or too low.
- **Median error.** The gap that half of the cars stay under. It is smaller than the mean, because a few big misses lift the mean.
- **Within 10%.** The share of cars priced inside 10% of the asking price.
- **Envelope.** The span of signed errors that holds 95% of the cars, and a darker span that holds 80%. Too low is a negative error, too high a positive one.
- **Range and confidence.** A model can give a range instead of one price. An 80% range should hold the real price 8 times in 10.


### The model side


- **General model (General LLM).** A large language model built to answer anything in words. You describe the car in a sentence and it replies with a price.
- **Prompt and example.** The prompt is the question we send. An example is a solved case placed in it. A prompt with 30 similar cars shows the model 30 listed cars and their prices first.
- **Fine-tuning.** Training a small language model further on your own rows. One pass reads every training car once.
- **Tabular model.** A model built for rows and columns. A large one is pre-trained on many tables and reads your table as context when it answers, with no training of its own.


**So what?** Three numbers carry this note: the mean error, the share within 10%, and the envelope. The rest measures them for three kinds of model.


## 3


The task and the data


The task is one line. Given the description of a car, return its asking price in euros.


### The data


- **14,463 listings from Belgian car dealers, snapshot of 16 Nov 2026.** One snapshot, taken on one day.
- **Used and new cars.** The 1,500 test cars hold 1,319 used cars and 181 new ones.
- **20 inputs per car.** Most describe the car: brand, model, fuel, gearbox, body type, power, mileage, age, CO2 and whether it is new. The others describe the listing and its seller.


### The split


- **11,963 training cars.** The fine-tuned model learns from these. The simple reference models use them too.
- **1,000 validation cars.** They choose the pass of training to keep.
- **1,500 test cars.** We gave them to no model as training rows, example or context. The tabular models and one CatBoost run see the training and validation cars together, 12,963 in all, as their context.


All models answer the same 1,500 cars. If a language model returns something we cannot read as a price, that car gets the median training price. That happened on 0 test cars for Fable and the fine-tuned runs we feature, and on 9 for the untrained Inkling 2 Mini.


### What a model sees for one car


A language model reads the car as a short text. A tabular model reads it as a row. Take the Volkswagen Golf we follow insection 6 : first registered in 2023, diesel, automatic, 85 kW, 57,186 km. Its asking price was hidden from every model.


### The floor


Some cars are identical on every input yet listed at different prices. We found 1,236 such cars in 387 groups. Inside a group, prices differ by 1.0% to 2.4%. No model can see why, so an error under 1% is out of reach with these inputs.


**So what?** This is the test a company would run on its own table: hide the answer on cases kept away from the model, ask for it, and score the gap. The floor tells you how low a good score can go.


## 4


Three kinds of model, five settings


We picked one model for each kind. For the two language models we also ran a setting that adds 30 similar cars to each question. That gives five settings.

### Who made what


- **Fable 5.2** is a general model from Anthropic. We called it at effort medium through the batch service, which charges 50% of the standard price.
- **Inkling 2 Mini** is part of Inkling, a model family from Thinking Machines Lab, tailored for its Tinker service. We fine-tuned it through Tinker.
- **TabPFN 3.5 Thinking** comes from Prior Labs. Its documentation says thinking mode runs only on the hosted service and suits batch predictions where quality matters more than fit time.
- **Kumo-Tabular Large** is a second tabular model. Its model card describes it as NVIDIA's pretrained tabular foundation model for classification and regression. It ran on our own Mac and it powers the price app insection 13 .


### The 30 similar cars


For each test car we chose 30 training cars by rule: the same brand and model first, then the same brand and body type, then the same body type and energy type.


All five settings answered the same 1,500 test cars. The fine-tuned model used the 1,000 validation cars to pick its pass and never saw a test car.


**So what?** The three kinds differ in what they learn from. A general model learns nothing from you. A fine-tuned model learns from your rows once. A tabular model reads your rows at the moment of each question.

- **The table model came first,** at 5.08% mean error. Half of its cars were off by 3.27% or less, and 83.9% landed within 10% of the asking price.

### Which gaps are real


A test of 1,500 cars has noise. We resampled the cars 10,000 times to see which gaps survive.


- **Table model against the general model with 30 cars: a real gap.** 0.96 points, with a 95% interval of 0.68 to 1.24 points. The gap is measured before rounding; the two rounded scores differ by 0.95.
- **Table model against the fine-tuned model with 30 cars: a real gap.** 1.18 points, interval 0.91 to 1.47. Here we compare with Kumo-Tabular Large, which scored the same 5.08% as TabPFN.
- **General model against fine-tuned model, both with 30 cars: not separated.** 0.23 points, interval minus 0.08 to plus 0.55. The test cannot tell them apart. Section 12 returns to this gap.

**FIG. 3.** For each setting, the band that holds 95% of the errors and the band that holds 80%, as a share of the asking price. The dashed line is a perfect price.


- **The table model has the narrowest envelope.** 95% of its errors lie between 16.1% too low and 15.8% too high. 80% lie between 9.1% too low and 7.8% too high.
- **The general model without examples leans high.** Its median error is 3.2% too high. 95% of its errors lie between 20.3% too low and 28.7% too high.
- **30 similar cars remove the lean.** Its median error falls to 0.0% and its 95% span to 17.8% too low and 18.1% too high.
- **The fine-tuned model sits in between.** Its 95% span runs from 20.0% too low to 19.1% too high. With 30 similar cars it narrows to 18.9% too low and 17.8% too high.


### By asking price


The second panel splits the cars by asking price. Under 15,000 EUR, 186 cars, the long tail of misses sits on the high side. The table model's 95% span runs from 11.8% too low to 19.5% too high. Over 40,000 EUR, 258 cars, the tail flips to the low side: from 27.3% too low to 14.6% too high. Between 15,000 and 25,000 EUR, 579 cars, the same model has its lowest mean error, 4.63%.


**So what?** Even the table model priced 1 car in 20 more than 15.8% too high or 16.1% too low. Read the envelope before you automate a decision on the answer.

### By age


- **New and nearly new cars are easiest.** For the 328 cars under 1 year old, the table model scores 4.05%, the general model with examples 4.40% and the fine-tuned model with examples 5.04%.
- **Old cars are hardest.** For the 89 cars aged 7 years or more, the same three settings score 6.89%, 9.04% and 8.85%.
- **New cars.** On the 181 new cars the general model without examples scores 10.39%. Adding 30 similar cars brings it to 3.76%, close to the table model at 3.53%.


### By how often the model is known


We counted how often each brand and model appears among the 11,963 training cars.


- **20 cars or more, 1,142 test cars.** Table model 4.61%, general model with examples 5.61%, fine-tuned model with examples 5.68%.
- **1 to 4 cars, 97 test cars.** 8.03%, 9.09% and 10.09%.
- **Not in the training cars, 22 test cars.** 10.17%, 9.47% and 14.47%. Here the general model without examples scored 9.28%, the lowest of the five. With 22 cars this is a hint and no verdict.


**So what?** Trust each model least where it has seen least. Check your own table for the rare cases, and route them to a person.


## 9


What 30 similar cars change


Putting solved cases into the question is the cheapest lever we tested. It needs no training.


- **General model.** Mean error fell from 10.09% to 6.03% with 30 similar cars. The share within 10% rose from 59.3% to 79.2%.
- **Fine-tuned model.** Mean error fell from 7.12% to 6.26%, a real gap of 0.86 points. The share within 10% rose from 73.1% to 77.5%.
- **The two now sit together.** At 6.03% and 6.26% the test cannot separate them.


The lever has a price. Each question is longer, so the general model's cost per car rose from $0.0042 to $0.019 at its standard price, and from $0.0021 to $0.0095 at the batch price we paid. For the fine-tuned model it rose from $0.000026 to $0.000228, and training from $4.21 to $41.26.


**So what?** If you use a general model, put 30 similar solved cases in each question. It moved our error by 4.06 points, at 4.5 times the cost per question.


## 10


What fine-tuning costs and gives


Fine-tuning teaches a small model your task. We tested what it takes, and 3 choices that might have made it better.


### Training works


An untrained Inkling 2 Mini, asked cold, scored 18.33% and failed to give a readable price on 9 of 1,500 cars. After 3 passes over the 11,963 training cars it scored 7.12%, with no failure. The training cost $4.21.


### A larger model did not help


Inkling 2 Small is the larger sibling. Trained for 6 passes with mileage per year added to the prompt, it scored 7.15% for $17.95. Against Mini at 7.12% the gap is 0.03 points, interval minus 0.38 to plus 0.44. The test cannot separate them. Writing mileage per year moved Small from 7.44% to 7.15%. That gap has an interval of minus 0.07 to plus 0.67 points, so the gain is not proven.


### Longer training did not help


We trained Mini for 8 passes instead of 3. The best pass on the validation cars was the seventh, and it scored 7.40% on the test cars for $11.44. The gap against 3 passes is 0.28 points, interval minus 0.11 to plus 0.69, so the test cannot separate them. From pass 6 on, some answers stopped being readable prices: 1 failed answer on the validation cars at pass 6, 3 at pass 7 and 5 at pass 8. The validation error rose again at pass 8.

**So what?** Training moved the error a long way. After 3 passes, 5 more passes and the next size up bought nothing we could separate from noise. Examples in the prompt moved it again.

**FIG. 5.** Each dot is one setting. Lower is better and further left is cheaper. The cost axis is logarithmic: each step to the right is ten times more. Fable 5.2 is plotted at its standard price; we paid the batch price, half of it.


### Cost per answer


- **General model: $0.0042** per car with no example and **$0.019** with 30 similar cars, at the standard price. We paid the batch price, which charges 50% of the standard price: $0.0021 and $0.0095.
- **Fine-tuned small, no example: $0.000026** per car, after $4.21 of training. **With 30 similar cars: $0.000228** , after $41.26.
- **Tabular models: $0 per prediction** on our own Mac for Kumo-Tabular Large, which took 407 seconds for the 1,500 cars. TabPFN 3.5 Thinking used free account credits on the vendor's hosted service and took 9 seconds.


For 1,000 answers the bill at the standard price is $19.00 from the general model with 30 cars, $4.20 without examples, and $0.228 from the fine-tuned model with 30 cars. Training is extra.


### Effort


- **General model:** write a prompt and a rule that picks 30 similar cars. No training.
- **Fine-tuned small:** prepare 11,963 training answers, run 3 passes, pick the best pass on 1,000 validation cars.
- **Tabular model:** hand over the table. We gave it 12,963 cars. No training.


**So what?** The tabular route has the lowest cost and the lowest error here. The next section sets the fine-tuned route against the general model.


## 12


A fine-tuned small model is level with Fable 5.2 and about 83 times cheaper per answer


The comparison holds a second result. Inkling 2 Mini, fine-tuned on our cars, is level with Fable 5.2 on error and costs far less to run. Both settings below get 30 similar cars in each question, and Fable 5.2 is priced at its full, standard rate.


Table 4 · Fable 5.2 at its standard price and fine-tuned Inkling 2 Mini, both with 30 similar cars in each question Measure Fable 5.2, general LLM Inkling 2 Mini, fine-tuned small Reading

### What level means


The gap is 0.23 points, with a 95% interval of minus 0.08 to plus 0.55 from 10,000 resamples of the 1,500 cars. The interval holds zero, so the test cannot separate the two. We read them as level. One caution comes from section 8: on the 22 test cars whose model is absent from the training cars, Fable 5.2 scored 9.47% and the fine-tuned model 14.47%. Treat it as a hint.


### What the ratio says, and what it costs to get there


At its standard price Fable 5.2 costs $0.019 per answer and the fine-tuned model $0.000228. The fine-tuned model is about 83 times cheaper per answer. The entry fee is the training: $41.26, paid once, for 3 passes with 30 similar cars in each prompt. Fable 5.2 needs none. The fine-tuned model saves $0.018772 on each answer, so the break-even volume is $41.26 / $0.018772 = 2,198 answers, computed by script from the cost figures. Below that volume the general model is cheaper in total. Above it the fine-tuned model is.


### What we paid


We called Fable 5.2 through the batch service, which charges half of the standard price: $0.0095 per answer. At that price the ratio is about 42 times cheaper per answer, and the break-even after $41.26 of training is 4,450 answers.


**So what?** If you ask the same question thousands of times, a fine-tuned small model can be level with a general model at about 83 times lower cost per answer at the general model's full price. It costs $41.26 to train and repays itself beyond 2,198 answers.

### Why the app says 6.30% and the result page says 5.08%


The two numbers answer different questions.


- **5.08% is the model ranking.** Every car carried all 20 inputs, including details of the listing and its seller.
- **6.30% is the app as a reader uses it.** A reader types a car and has no seller details. The app treats the car as listed today and fills the energy type from the fuel.
- **The same model, measured in four runs.** On the same 1,500 cars, Kumo-Tabular Large scored 5.06% with all 20 inputs and 6.21% with no seller details. The form as shipped scored 6.30%. The ranking run, also with all 20 inputs, scored 5.08%. The 5.06% and the 5.08% are two separate runs of the same model.


**So what?** Ask any price tool for a range, then check how often reality lands inside it. A range that holds 8 prices in 10 at 80% is one you can build a rule on.

### Five moves for Monday


If you own a prediction from a table, do these in order.


1. **Pick one table** with past cases and their outcomes. We worked with 12,963 cars.
2. **Hold out test cases.** We hid 1,500 from every model. No candidate may see them.
3. **Run a tabular model first.** Hand it the table. It needs no training.
4. **Run a general model with 30 similar cases** in each question, and price each answer.
5. **Ask for a range and check it.** Count how often reality lands inside. Decide on fine-tuning only after you know your volume of questions.


**So what?** One honest test on your own table decides the kind of model. Run it before you sign for any of the three.


## 16


The fine print


- **One market, one snapshot, one split.** The result covers 14,463 listings from Belgian car dealers on 16 Nov 2026, with one random split. A second split can move the order of close models.
- **Asking prices are not sale prices.** The target is the price on the listing.
- **20 inputs, no condition.** No input holds damage, service history or an options list.
- **Different training cars.** The tabular models and one CatBoost run see 12,963 cars. The fine-tuned models train on 11,963 and use 1,000 validation cars to choose the pass.
- **Different ways of predicting.** TabPFN-3.5-Thinking predicts the price in euros and was tuned by the vendor's service on the percentage error. The local tabular models predict the logarithm of the price.
- **Costs** come from the token counts of each run and the vendor's price on the run date. Fable 5.2 is shown at its standard price. We paid the batch price, half of it, which makes the fine-tuned model about 42 times cheaper per answer, with a break-even of 4,450 answers after $41.26 of training. For models on our own Mac we show machine time and did not count the Mac's cost.
- **TabPFN's credits.** The free account showed 151,095 of 5,000,000 credits used after the run, That reading covers all use of the account, so the run itself used no more than that.
- **Not scored.** Mitra, a tabular model from AutoGluon, was not scored: we found no practical way to run it on our Mac.


**So what?** Treat the result as a strong signal on one market and one snapshot. Rerun it on your own table before you decide.
